articles.title: Building Sustainability In, Not Adding It Later
articles.standfirst: What working with existing buildings has taught me about decisions made long before the facilities team arrives
articles.body:
Working in facilities management has changed the way I think about buildings.

When a building is handed over to the team responsible for running it, a great deal has already been decided. Its orientation is fixed, materials have been selected, cooling and water systems are installed, and lighting has been specified.

In many cases, the decisions that will influence how much energy the building consumes and how expensive it is to operate were made years before the facilities team became involved.

Of course, there is still a lot that can be improved during operation. Equipment can be managed differently, maintenance practices can change, inefficient lighting can be replaced, and energy consumption can be monitored more closely.

I have seen the value of those interventions firsthand but I have also started asking a different question.

> What if some of the problems we spend time correcting later could have been avoided by making better decisions earlier?

## A lesson from Benin City Mall

That question became more important to me in 2025 while I was working with Knight Frank Nigeria.

At Benin City Mall, I took the initiative to investigate persistent operating losses. I wanted to understand where the building was using more electricity than it needed as energy costs were putting pressure on the property and its tenants.

The review pointed to two significant areas: cooling and lighting.

Air-conditioning systems were operating overnight in parts of the mall with little or no activity, while older lighting fixtures were consuming more electricity than necessary. Together, these accounted for 62% of the energy waste identified in our assessment.

We adjusted how the cooling systems were operated and replaced inefficient lighting. Within six months, energy consumption had fallen by 27%.

That result mattered but what stayed with me was the larger lesson behind it.

We had found ways to make an existing building perform better. Yet we were still working within the boundaries of decisions that had already been made.

We could change when an air-conditioning system operated or replace a light fitting but there are other decisions that become much harder and sometimes much more expensive, to change once a building is complete.

That is where my interest in sustainability began to move beyond facilities management.

## Some problems are easier to prevent than correct

Consider cooling.

If a building is designed in a way that increases heat gain, the consequence may be greater reliance on mechanical cooling throughout its life. The facilities team can operate that system more efficiently but it cannot easily change the building's orientation.

The same applies to water. If water efficiency is overlooked when systems and fixtures are selected, future operators inherit the consequences.

Materials matter too. What looks like an attractive decision during construction may create different maintenance, replacement or environmental costs over time.

These issues made me realise that building performance is not simply an operational concern. It is shaped throughout the development process.

Nigeria's growing green-building market reflects a similar idea. The International Finance Corporation's Nigeria EDGE Green Buildings Market Transformation Program has focused on reducing energy and water consumption, as well as the energy embodied in construction materials. The programme links those improvements not only to a lower-carbon development path but also to lower utility bills and operating costs. [disclosures.ifc.org](https://disclosures.ifc.org/project-detail/AS/603764/projectname-pending), [disclosures.ifc.org](https://disclosures.ifc.org/project-detail/AS/603764/nigeria-edge-green-buildings-market-transformation-program)

That combination is important to me because the case for sustainability becomes much more practical when environmental performance and commercial performance are considered together.

## Sustainability also has to make financial sense

Property owners, developers and investors do not make decisions in a vacuum.

Capital is limited, returns matter, occupancy matters, maintenance costs matter, so do financing conditions and long-term asset performance.

I don't believe sustainability should ignore those realities.

My experience at Benin City Mall taught me that an environmental improvement can become easier to implement when the people making the decision can also understand the economics behind it.

The conversation changes when we can move from:

*This will use less energy.*

to:

*This will use less energy, this is what it will cost, this is what it could save and this is how long the investment could take to pay for itself.*

That does not mean every environmental decision needs to produce an immediate financial return. Many important questions, particularly those involving resilience, climate risk and social impact are more complicated than a simple payback calculation.

But where environmental and financial value can reinforce each other, we should be able to demonstrate it.

There are signs that this thinking is gaining ground in Nigeria. In 2025, Green Building Council Nigeria and Sintali announced a partnership aimed at expanding adoption of EDGE, including awareness, capacity building and practical support for developers and professionals. [von.gov.ng](https://von.gov.ng/nigeria-takes-bold-step-towards-greener-buildings/)

The opportunity is therefore not purely theoretical.

> What should we build differently?

Nigeria and other African markets will continue to need homes, offices, retail spaces, schools, hospitals and infrastructure.

Every new project creates decisions that may remain with the asset for decades.

How much energy will the building require?

How much water?

How will it respond to hotter conditions or heavier rainfall?

How expensive will it be to operate?

What will occupants inherit from decisions they had no part in making?

Those questions should not begin after the keys have been handed to the facilities team.

Existing buildings will always require good management. They will need maintenance, retrofits, monitoring and continuous improvement. My own professional experience has shown me how much value those interventions can create but it has also made me more interested in what comes before them.

When I encounter an inefficient system now, I try to ask two questions:

> How can we improve this?

And then:

> What could have been done earlier so that we did not inherit this problem in the first place?

That second question is increasingly shaping the direction I want my work to take.

I still care about making existing buildings perform better but over time, I want to contribute earlier, while the decisions that determine environmental and financial performance can still be shaped.

Sometimes the best retrofit may be the one we never need to make.

articles.title: When Sustainability Makes Financial Sense
articles.standfirst: What one property taught me about making environmental improvements easier for decision-makers to support
articles.body:
One of my most useful lessons about sustainability started with a very different problem.

Money.

In 2025, while working with Knight Frank Nigeria, I took the initiative to investigate persistent losses at Benin City Mall. The property was losing approximately USD3,200 each month and energy expenditure was contributing to the pressure.

There was an obvious temptation to ask for more money.

I thought we should first understand where the existing money was going and that decision eventually changed the way I think about sustainability.

## Start with the problem, not the label

Our review of the mall's electricity use identified unnecessary overnight cooling in areas with little or no activity. We also found older lighting fixtures using more electricity than necessary.

Together, cooling and lighting accounted for 62% of the energy waste identified in our assessment.

At that point, we knew where much of the problem was coming from but identifying waste and getting someone to pay to correct it are two very different things.

The state government still had to decide whether investing more capital made sense.

That required me to change the way I presented the solution.

Instead of relying on a technical explanation of inefficient cooling and lighting, I translated the recommendations into financial terms. The proposed investment had an estimated payback period of fourteen months, with projected savings of approximately USD13,714 over three years.

Now there was something concrete to discuss.

With stakeholder support, unnecessary overnight cooling was reduced and inefficient lighting replaced.

Within six months, energy consumption had fallen by 27%, while realised cumulative operating-cost savings reached approximately USD2,133.

For me, the important lesson wasn't simply that we saved energy. It was that an environmental improvement became easier to support when the commercial case was visible too.

## The questions decision-makers actually ask

When sustainability is discussed among people who already care deeply about environmental issues, it is easy to forget what the conversation sounds like elsewhere.

A property owner might agree completely that reducing energy consumption is desirable and still ask:

> How much will this cost?

> How long before I recover the investment?

> Will the work interrupt operations?

> What happens to my operating expenses?

> Will occupants notice an improvement?

> How will we measure whether it worked?

Those are not unreasonable objections to sustainability. They are normal investment questions.

And if we want more environmental improvements to move from proposals into actual buildings, we need to get better at answering them.

That is why I increasingly believe that the financial case should sit alongside the environmental case, not behind it.

The International Finance Corporation's Nigeria EDGE Green Buildings Market Transformation Program takes a similar market-oriented approach. Its objectives include reducing energy and water consumption and the energy embodied in construction materials while lowering utility costs for homeowners and operating costs for businesses. [disclosures.ifc.org](https://disclosures.ifc.org/project-detail/AS/603764/projectname-pending), [disclosures.ifc.org](https://disclosures.ifc.org/project-detail/AS/603764/nigeria-edge-green-buildings-market-transformation-program)

Nigeria's green-building market is also beginning to produce more visible examples. Projects recognised through IFC EDGE have included office, retail and mixed-use properties, as well as retrofits of existing assets. [guardian.ng](https://guardian.ng/news/ifc-edge-recognises-new-green-building-projects-at-future-cities-africa-green-building-summit/)

What interests me about this is not certification for its own sake. It is the possibility of making better building performance measurable because what gets measured becomes much easier to discuss.

## Before recommending a solution, establish the baseline

The Benin City Mall experience also changed the questions I ask when looking at a property.

Before talking about solutions, I increasingly want to know:

How much energy does the building currently consume?

Where is that energy going?

How much water does it use?

What does poor performance cost?

Where is waste occurring?

What environmental or climate risks affect the property?

Which improvements are technically realistic?

How much will they cost?

And after implementation, what will tell us whether they worked?

Without a baseline, sustainability can easily become a collection of good intentions. With one, we have something to test.

## From one building to a repeatable approach

This thinking is now informing a sustainability advisory model I am developing for the built environment.

The approach I'm exploring is deliberately straightforward:

> Establish the baseline. Diagnose the problem. Prioritise the opportunities. Build the business case. Implement. Measure. Learn.

The aim isn't to recommend every sustainability intervention available.

A particular building may need to focus on energy first. Another may have a more serious water problem. Somewhere else, drainage, waste, resilience or occupant needs may be more pressing.

The point is to understand the asset before prescribing the solution and then to ask which interventions make sense environmentally, operationally and financially.

## Making better decisions easier to approve

Not every environmental benefit can or should be reduced to a financial return.

Climate resilience is a good example. The value of avoiding future disruption may not fit neatly into a fourteen-month payback calculation. The same is true of many social and environmental outcomes.

But that should not stop us from quantifying value where we genuinely can.

If a more efficient building can reduce resource consumption, lower operating expenditure and improve performance, decision-makers should be able to see those relationships clearly.

My work at Benin City Mall started with a fairly ordinary question:

> Where are we losing money?

It has since led me towards a much bigger one:

> How can we make environmentally responsible decisions easier for property owners, investors and institutions to justify?

I don't have a complete answer yet.

That's part of what I'm trying to build.

What I know from experience is that good intentions alone rarely change buildings. Someone eventually has to approve the investment, implement the solution and measure what happened.

If sustainability is going to become a more normal part of how we develop and operate property in Nigeria, those conversations will have to work for more than environmental specialists.

They will have to make sense to the people signing the cheque too.

articles.title: The Blank Slate Advantage: Can Africa Leapfrog to a More Sustainable Built Environment?
articles.standfirst: We do not always have to catch up. In some areas, we can build differently from the start.
articles.body:
When I first wrote about the **“Blank Slate Advantage”** in September 2025, I was thinking about what looks, at first, like one of Africa's biggest disadvantages: the scale of infrastructure we still need to build.

Homes, offices, hospitals, schools, retail spaces, transport infrastructure, entire neighbourhoods and cities will have to expand to accommodate a rapidly urbanising population.

The scale of that challenge is enormous. Africa's urban population is projected to grow from about 700 million to 1.4 billion by 2050, meaning that the continent's cities will need to accommodate roughly 700 million additional residents over the next three decades. [citiesalliance.org](https://www.citiesalliance.org/resources/publications/publications/africas-urbanisation-dynamics-2025-planning-africas-urban), [issuu.com](https://issuu.com/swac-oecd/docs/aud-2024-highlights)

But I have started to see another side to this story.

Infrastructure that has not yet been built also represents **decisions that have not yet been made**.

What materials will we use? How will buildings be cooled? Where will their energy come from? How much water will they consume? How will they cope with heat, flooding or unreliable utilities? And how expensive will they be to operate twenty or thirty years after construction?

That is what I mean by the **Blank Slate Advantage**.

Not that Africa is literally a blank slate. It isn't. Our cities already contain ageing buildings, infrastructure deficits and systems that urgently need investment. Many existing assets will have to be repaired, upgraded and retrofitted.

My argument is slightly different.

Where we need to build anyway, we have an opportunity to make some of these decisions differently from the beginning.

## Learning from the cost of fixing things later

Working in facilities management has made this idea much more concrete for me.

Facilities teams frequently receive buildings after the important choices have already been made. The orientation is fixed. Cooling systems have been installed. Materials selected. Lighting systems specified. Water infrastructure designed.

We can improve how those systems operate, and sometimes the results can be significant.

At Benin City Mall, for example, an assessment I led identified avoidable energy waste associated with cooling and lighting. Changes to operating practices and lighting subsequently contributed to a 27% reduction in energy consumption.

That experience showed me the value of improving existing buildings.

But it also left me wondering:

> What if some of the inefficiencies facilities teams spend years managing could have been avoided at the design and development stage?

That question has gradually changed how I think about Africa's infrastructure challenge.

## Leapfrogging should be practical, not rhetorical

“Leapfrogging” is an attractive word.

It can also become meaningless if we don't explain what it looks like in practice.

For the built environment, I think it begins with relatively straightforward questions.

Can passive design reduce a building's dependence on mechanical cooling?

Can water efficiency be considered before plumbing systems and fixtures are specified?

Can drainage and flood resilience be designed around the climate conditions a development is likely to face over its lifetime?

Can building-management systems measure energy and water consumption from the beginning rather than being added years later?

Can developers assess the long-term operating consequences of material and equipment choices, rather than focusing mainly on initial cost?

None of these ideas is revolutionary on its own.

The opportunity lies in making them normal.

## Africa's solar opportunity illustrates the point

Energy is perhaps the clearest example.

Africa has around 60% of the world's best solar resources but has historically accounted for only a very small share of installed global solar photovoltaic capacity. [mg.co.za](https://mg.co.za/the-green-guardian/2026-11-20-global-energy-crisis-sharpens-africa-s-push-for-electricity-access/), [energyinst.org](https://knowledge.energyinst.org/new-energy-world/article?id=127558)

That gap is frustrating, but it also illustrates the scale of the opportunity.

For a new facility, the question does not necessarily need to be:

*How do we add renewable energy later?*

It can be:

> How should energy be considered from the beginning?

Solar will not be the right answer for every building or every location. Neither should renewable energy distract from reducing demand in the first place.

A building that wastes energy does not become efficient simply because solar panels are installed on the roof.

The sequence matters.

First, understand demand.

Reduce avoidable consumption.

Design for efficiency.

Then determine how renewable energy fits the operating requirements and economics of the asset.

That is a more useful definition of leapfrogging than simply installing newer technology.

## Born with data, not made smart later

The same principle applies to building technology.

When I originally wrote about this idea, I used the phrase **“born digital, not retrofitted.”** I still believe in the principle, although I now think about it less in terms of technology for technology's sake.

A genuinely smart building should help people make better decisions.

That could mean installing energy and water metering that shows where resources are being consumed. It could as well mean using building-management systems to adjust equipment schedules to actual demand or identifying faults early enough to prevent larger failures.

Over time, reliable building-performance data also gives owners something they often lack: a baseline.

Without knowing how a building performs today, it becomes difficult to prove that an intervention improved it tomorrow.

Digital systems therefore matter not because artificial intelligence, sensors or smart buildings sound futuristic, but because **better information can lead to better decisions**.

## Resilience cannot be added as an afterthought either

Sustainability also means preparing buildings for the conditions in which they will actually operate.

Across African cities, those conditions can include extreme heat, heavy rainfall, flooding, water constraints and unreliable energy supply.

A building can be beautiful and still perform poorly when those realities are ignored.

Resilience therefore needs to move closer to the beginning of development decisions.

How will water leave the site during intense rainfall?

How will indoor temperatures be managed during extreme heat?

What happens if grid electricity becomes unavailable?

Can the building continue functioning during disruption?

These are design and investment questions before they become facilities-management problems.

## But someone still has to pay for it

This is where my thinking has changed most since I first wrote about the Blank Slate Advantage.

It is easy to say Africa should build sustainably.

It is harder to answer the next question:

> How do we persuade the people financing and developing these assets to make different choices?

Good intentions are not a business case.

Developers, investors and property owners have to consider capital costs, operating expenditure, financing, occupancy, risk and returns.

Sustainability therefore has a much better chance of being adopted when its environmental benefits can be considered alongside its commercial implications.

That does not mean every climate or environmental decision needs a short payback period.

Some benefits, particularly resilience and avoided future risk, are difficult to reduce to a simple financial calculation.

But where we can demonstrate that reducing energy or water consumption also lowers operating costs, improves building performance or avoids future corrective expenditure, we should.

The International Finance Corporation's EDGE programme reflects this connection between resource efficiency and commercial outcomes. Its work in Nigeria has focused on reducing energy and water consumption and the energy embodied in construction materials while also reducing utility and operating costs. [disclosures.ifc.org](https://disclosures.ifc.org/project-detail/AS/603764/projectname-pending), [disclosures.ifc.org](https://disclosures.ifc.org/project-detail/AS/603764/nigeria-edge-green-buildings-market-transformation-program)

That combination matters.

Sustainability becomes much easier to scale when it makes sense to the people responsible for approving and financing it.

## The people living with our decisions

There is another reason why getting these choices right matters.

The people who experience a building do not necessarily choose how it was designed. An office worker does not select the cooling system. A tenant does not determine the building's orientation.

A family buying or renting a home may have had no influence over its water efficiency, insulation or materials. Communities living around developments may not have determined how drainage, waste or environmental risks were considered.

Yet people ultimately live with those decisions, sometimes for decades.

That is where sustainability becomes a question of **climate justice** as well as engineering and finance.

The consequences of poor development decisions are not always borne by the people who made them.

If Africa is going to build at the scale its urban growth requires, we should care not only about how much infrastructure we create, but also about **who inherits the consequences of the choices we make today**.

> So, can Africa leapfrog?

I believe we can in some areas.

But I think the answer requires more humility than my original statement implied.

Africa cannot simply skip every stage of development. We face difficult constraints around financing, skills, regulation, infrastructure, technology and institutional capacity. Some existing assets will need expensive retrofits regardless of what we do next.

And sustainability itself has trade-offs.

The newest technology is not automatically the most appropriate. A green certification does not guarantee that a building will perform well in practice. Solar panels cannot compensate for fundamentally wasteful design. Imported sustainability solutions will not always fit local climatic, economic or social realities.

Leapfrogging will therefore require more than adopting what other markets have already developed.

It will require learning from them, adapting what works and being willing to design solutions around African conditions.

That is the opportunity I see.

Africa's infrastructure deficit is real. But many of the buildings and systems we will rely on in 2050 have not yet been built.

That means many important decisions have not yet been locked in either.

We may not have a completely blank slate.

But we still have space to choose differently.

> The question is what we decide to build on it.

*An earlier version of this idea was published on my LinkedIn page on September 8, 2025. This article revisits the Blank Slate Advantage with updated evidence and reflections from my subsequent work in the built environment.*

articles.title: Who Pays When We Build Unsustainably?
articles.standfirst: The people who live with development decisions are not always the people who make them
articles.body:
A building begins with decisions.

Someone decides where it will sit, how it will be oriented, what materials will be used, how it will be cooled, how water will be managed and what level of resilience is worth paying for.

Eventually, those decisions become concrete, steel, glass, pipes and equipment.

Then somebody else inherits them.

A tenant inherits the electricity bill. A facilities team inherits the cooling system. A business inherits the disruption when drainage fails. A household inherits the cost of keeping an inefficient home comfortable.

That gap between **who makes a decision and who lives with its consequences** has become increasingly important to how I think about the built environment.

It also raises a question that I believe should sit closer to the centre of sustainability discussions:

> When we build badly, who actually pays?

## The obvious cost is not always the real cost

Construction decisions are often evaluated around the cost of delivering a project.

I understand why. Budgets matter.

But the amount required to construct a building is only one part of what that building will eventually cost.

Consider cooling.

A decision that appears economical during design may result in a building that depends heavily on mechanical air-conditioning. Once occupied, that decision becomes an electricity bill that arrives month after month.

The developer may no longer own the property. The consultant may have moved to another project.

But the building is still consuming energy, the occupant is still paying, and facilities team is still trying to make the system work more efficiently.

This is one of the reasons my experience in facilities management has changed the way I look at development decisions. Facilities teams often meet a building at the point where earlier choices become operating realities.

And by then, some choices are expensive to change.

## Think about water

The same principle applies to water.

If water efficiency is considered early, developers can make choices around fixtures, metering, rainwater harvesting or reuse systems while designing the building.

But if ignored, the implications do not disappear.

They simply show up later as consumption, cost or pressure on supply.

Again, the person dealing with the consequence may not be the person who made the original decision.

## Then there is resilience

This becomes even more serious when we think about climate risk.

Imagine a commercial property in an area exposed to increasingly intense rainfall.

Drainage may look like one line in a development budget. But if the provision is inadequate, the hidden cost could eventually include flooding, damaged equipment, interrupted businesses, repairs, lost income and rising insurance costs.

And the impact does not necessarily stop at the property boundary.

Poorly considered development can affect surrounding drainage, traffic, access and communities.

The cheapest decision today can become someone else's expensive problem tomorrow.

That does not mean every project needs the most sophisticated or expensive solution available.

It means cost needs a longer memory.

## This is where climate justice becomes practical

For a long time, I associated climate justice primarily with large global questions: which countries produced the most emissions, which countries are most vulnerable, and who should finance the transition.

Those questions are important.

But I increasingly see a much more local version of climate justice in the built environment.

A person does not have to participate in a development decision to experience its consequences.

An office worker may have no influence over whether their workplace has adequate cooling or natural ventilation.

A tenant may have had no say in how energy-efficient a building is but still pays service charges linked to its performance.

A family may have had no role in designing the drainage around their neighbourhood but lives with the consequences when heavy rainfall comes.

The relationship is not always simple, and not every environmental problem can be traced to one decision-maker.

Still, the principle matters.

> The ability to make a decision and the ability to escape its consequences are not always held by the same people.

That, to me, is one of the practical questions climate justice asks of the built environment.

## Better buildings need broader questions

When assessing a development choice, perhaps we should ask more than:

> What will this cost to build?

We could also ask:

> What will it cost to operate?

> What resources will it consume?

> How will it perform during extreme weather?

> Who will pay when its systems are inefficient?

> Who carries the risk if our assumptions turn out to be wrong?

> How difficult will this decision be to reverse later?

These questions do not replace financial discipline. They improve it.

They encourage us to look at cost across the life of an asset rather than only at the point of construction.

And they bring people back into a sustainability conversation that can otherwise become dominated by certifications, technology and carbon calculations.

## Sustainability should not become a luxury

There is another danger I think we need to acknowledge.

If sustainable buildings are treated primarily as premium products for organisations that can afford expensive technology and certification, we risk making the transition itself unequal.

Efficient lighting is useful because it uses less energy, not because it carries a sustainability label.

Passive cooling matters because it can reduce dependence on mechanical systems.

Water efficiency matters because water is a resource, whether the building has a green certification or not.

Good drainage matters because people need buildings and communities that can continue functioning when it rains heavily.

The goal should not simply be to build impressive “green buildings.”

It should be to make **better building performance increasingly normal**.

> Who pays?

This is the question I keep coming back to.

When we choose an inefficient cooling system, who pays?

When water is wasted, who pays?

When drainage is inadequate, who pays?

When a building needs an expensive retrofit ten years after completion, who pays?

Sometimes it is the owner.

Sometimes it is the tenant.

Sometimes it is a business.

Sometimes the cost is absorbed by a community or a public institution.

Sometimes the environmental cost is harder to see.

But somebody usually inherits the decision.

That is why I think sustainability needs to enter the conversation earlier.

Not because every building can be perfect nor because every environmental consideration outweighs every financial one.

But because the choices we make about buildings can remain long after the people who made them have moved on.

If we think more carefully about **who eventually pays**, we may make better decisions about what, how and for whom we build.

articles.title: What a Beach Cleanup in Accra Changed About the Way I See the Built Environment
articles.standfirst: Sometimes an experience does not give you an answer. It simply changes the questions you start asking.
articles.imageCaption: Waste along the Accra shoreline. Photo: Tide Turners cleanup.
articles.body:
I did not go to Accra expecting a beach cleanup to change the way I thought about real estate.

I was there in 2025 and had joined a cleanup organised with The OR Foundation. Our task was practical: clear fashion and plastic waste from the shoreline.

For me, however, simply being beside the water meant something else.

Years earlier, I had lost my best friend to drowning at Elegushi Beach in Lagos. Afterwards, I stopped going to beaches and avoided large bodies of water.

It wasn't a decision I spent much time analysing. Staying away was easier.

Then, years later, I found myself standing on another West African coastline, picking waste from the shore.

I had returned to somewhere I had taught myself to avoid.

But what stayed with me afterwards wasn't simply the fact that I went back.

It was what I noticed while I was there.

## Looking beyond the clean-up

As we worked along the shoreline, my attention moved towards Jamestown and the communities around the coast.

My relationship with the water was personal. I could leave at the end of the clean-up. I could return home and, if I wanted, continue avoiding beaches altogether.

For people whose homes, work or daily lives are tied to the coastline, that relationship is different.

That distinction stayed with me.

I want to be cautious about what I claim from one experience. Spending time at a beach clean-up did not suddenly make me an expert on Jamestown, coastal livelihoods or environmental vulnerability in Ghana.

What it did was make me question something I had previously understood mostly in the abstract.

People do not experience environmental problems from equal positions.

The ability to distance yourself from an environmental problem is itself a form of choice.

Not everyone has it.

## I started noticing the same question elsewhere

When I returned to my professional world, that thought followed me.

Buildings are full of decisions that most occupants never make. Different people determine the materials, lighting, cooling system operations, drainage designs, usage of water and the level of efficiency or resilience worth paying for.

However, these are not the eventual occupants the building.

The eventual occupants work, shop and live in the building. They also pay energy bills or service charges, experience the indoor temperature however way it is, and deal with interruptions when systems fail.

The parallel is not perfect, and I would not pretend that a commercial building and a coastal community present the same challenge.

But the same question began to interest me:

> How much influence do people have over the environmental conditions they eventually inherit?

That question has stayed with me.

## Sustainability became less abstract

Before then, I would usually encounter sustainability through familiar professional language.

Energy efficiency, water conservation, waste management, building systems and operating costs.

These things remain important, and my work in facilities management has made that very clear but the clean-up gave those terms another dimension.

Energy efficiency affects bills, water systems affect availability and cost. Drainage systems and waste management affects individuals and businesses, while cooling sytems affects comfort, productivity and, increasingly, how people cope with weather conditions.

A sustainability decision eventually reaches a person somewhere.

Once I started thinking in those terms, sustainability became less about adding environmental features to buildings and more about asking **what consequences our decisions create, and who will live with them**.

## It also made me reconsider my role

Facilities management often involves inheriting decisions.

By the time a facilities team assumes responsibility for a building, much of its physical form has already been determined.

We can optimise, repair, adjust operating schedules, monitor consumption, and make a financial case for replacing inefficient systems.

However, these changes can produce substantial results.

The shoreline experience, together with my professionalism, made me more interested in what happens before that point.

Who decides how a building should perform?

When are environmental risks considered?

How early do operating costs enter the conversation?

Do we think enough about the people who will eventually use the asset?

And what would change if sustainability influenced some of those decisions before construction rather than being introduced mainly as a correction afterwards?

I did not have complete answers.

I still don't, but I began asking different questions.

## Returning to the water

Looking back, I think that is why the Accra experience remains important to me.

Going back to the coastline was personal, and working there shifted my attention outward.

I arrived with my own history with water. I left thinking more about other people's relationships with the environments around them.

It would be too neat to say that one afternoon created my interest in sustainability. It didn't.

My professional experiences, education and subsequent work have shaped that interest too.

What the clean-up did was give me another lens through which to look at things I was already beginning to encounter professionally.

Buildings are not simply assets, infrastructure is not simply capital expenditure and environmental performance is not simply a metric. However, people live inside the consequences of the decisions we make.

That idea now sits quietly behind many of the questions I ask about the built environment.

When we design, invest, operate or develop, **who gets to make the decision?**

Who benefits from it?

Who pays for it over time?

And who has the least ability to walk away if we get it wrong?

I went to the shoreline to help clear waste and I left with better questions.

For me, that has proved far more useful than pretending I came away with all the answers.
